phrases: Chayei Sarah ends with two families leaving Avraham’s house: the sons of Keturah, sent east with “gifts,” and Yishmael, whose twelve sons settle “before all his brothers.” Rav Tzadok and the Izhbitzer read both endings as a question about wisdom that lives outside the house of Avraham: what Avraham gave it, why he sent it away, and how it comes back. The shiur follows that question from a puzzling midrash to its answer, and then into later generations.

The main text is interlinear, phrase by phrase: each short Hebrew phrase is followed by its English in bold. For Pri Tzaddik, Mei HaShiloach, Beis Yaakov, Kometz HaMinchah and Divrei Soferim, the English follows Akiva Publishing’s translations, cut to match each phrase. The pesukim, the Gemara and Pri Tzaddik, Mishpatim 4 are newly translated, with abbreviations written out. The paragraphs between the sources explain them.

Tap a numbered marker beside the Hebrew to open its footnote, and tap a source named in a footnote to read that passage beside the shiur. In the paragraphs of Part X, the numbers open their notes the same way. The footnotes bring supporting sources from across the Kisvei Rav Tzadok library, and from other seforim that say the same things: kabbalah (the Zohar, Zohar Chadash, Recanati and the Shelah), machshavah (the Maharal, Ramban, Malbim and Taz), chassidus (Me’or Einayim, Kedushas Levi, Tanya, Arvei Nachal and Shem MiShmuel) and mussar (Avos and Mesillas Yesharim). Settings switches between Hebrew, English and both. The same shiur is also here page by page, as a PDF and as a Word file.

en: Avraham again took a wife, and her name was Keturah.

In Midrash Tanchuma (Chayei Sarah 8): “And Avraham again took a wife, and her name was Keturah” (Bereishis 25:1) – this is what the pasuk says: “Though your beginning was small, your latter end will greatly increase” (Iyov 8:7), and so on. At a hundred years he fathered one son (Yitzchak); so you must say: “though your beginning was small” – this is Avraham; “your latter end will greatly increase” – for he married a wife and fathered with her several sons at the end. Now this is astounding: he expounded “your beginning was small” of Yitzchak our father, peace be upon him, from whom came forth the whole nation of Israel, and of the sons of Keturah, who were idol worshippers, he expounded “your latter end will greatly increase”?!

This question drives the shiur. Yitzchak is the father of Israel, yet the Midrash calls him the “small beginning,” and calls the sons of Keturah the “great increase.” Rav Tzadok answers it only at the end of his ois, and we will too. First he asks what Avraham gave these sons and where he sent them.

The Gemara’s answer seems to make the question harder. Would Avraham hand his sons a name of impurity?
Now it is difficult to say

So the gift was holy. Avraham knew where his sons were going, and he gave them a Name that would still work there, so that something of Avraham would survive in them. The Beis Yaakov reads the same words from the side of the one who receives.
“And to the sons of the concubines that Avraham had,
Avraham gave gifts,” and so on.
“He handed them a name of impurity.”
that in truth, from Hashem’s side,

The two readings agree that the gift came from Hashem through Avraham. Pri Tzaddik speaks of what Avraham planted in his sons. Beis Yaakov speaks of the one who receives it: a gift received as one’s own achievement becomes a “name of impurity.” Both end with the same distance, east of Yitzchak. The next question is what was waiting in the East.

rich.text: Where is “the land of the East”? ⁧קֶדֶם⁩  (kedem) means “east,” and also “front” or “before,” because the ancients oriented themselves facing the sunrise. (The Midrash in Part III plays on ⁧מִזְרָח⁩ , “east,” literally the place where the sun shines.) In Tanach the Bnei Kedem are the peoples of the desert lands east and northeast of Eretz Yisrael, across the Yarden and out toward the Euphrates. On a modern map that is roughly eastern Jordan, Syria, northern Saudi Arabia and western Iraq. The pesukim place them this way:
Yaakov, on his way to Lavan in Charan (near today’s border of Turkey and Syria): ⁧וַיִּשָּׂא יַעֲקֹב רַגְלָיו⁩
and went to the land of the Bnei Kedem
Bilam, from Pesor on the Euphrates (Bamidbar 22:5): ⁧מִן אֲרָם יַנְחֵנִי בָלָק⁩
the greatest of all the Bnei Kedem
Desert raiders, together with Keturah’s son Midian: ⁧וְעָלָה מִדְיָן וַעֲמָלֵק⁩
); and together with Yishmael’s son Kedar: ⁧קוּמוּ עֲלוּ אֶל קֵדָר,⁩

Keturah’s sons fit this map. Midian (25:2) lived in northwest Arabia, east of the Gulf of Aqaba, and Dedan (25:3) was an oasis in the same region. Avraham sent them from Chevron southeast and east, into the Arabian desert, where their families mixed with the sons of Yishmael (see the note on milah in Part III).

The setting in the Gemara: the sons of Yishmael and of Keturah came before Alexander of Macedon to claim a share in Eretz Yisrael. Geviha ben Pesisa answered from these pesukim: a father who gave gifts to his sons in his lifetime and sent them away from one another, does one have any claim on the other? The Gemara then asks what the gifts were.
The Maharal asks the same question and answers that the gift was for removing sorcery, not using it (
that he gave them sorcery to use,
and a demon that entered a person – to drive it out;
for the Torah made death the penalty
for one who deals in sorcery.

Rashi on Bereishis 25:6 brings the Gemara as “a name of impurity.” Pri Tzaddik cites the reading ⁧שֵׁם בְּטוּמְאָה⁩  (“a Name in impurity”) from the Pa’aneach Raza and from Rashi on the Chumash; printed texts vary. The Baalei HaTosafos read it the same way (
and it would not harm them.
Chizkuni says the same. Sorcery is one of the prohibitions of Bnei Noach (Sanhedrin 56b), so Avraham could not have given them a name for sorcery.
The Shelah reads “shem tumah” the same way: holiness at the root, impurity only in the spreading out (
in the word “pilagshim” being written without a yud,
for the kelipah at its root is a Name,
and in its spreading out, impurity;
This is hinted in the word “pilagshim”:
that is, half of it is a Name;
but in the future it will be repaired,
for the impurity will be nullified.

Here the Beis Yaakov brings the Zohar (Tetzaveh 180b) on three kinds of names: supernal holy names that stand through the will of the spirit and heart, without speech; lower holy names that stand through speech and the intention drawn to them; and names of the Other Side, which stand only through an action below, “like Bilam and those people of the East.”

Applied to our time (this is an application, not the Beis Yaakov’s own words). His test does not depend on what a practice is called, but on whether the one who receives it ties it back to the Giver. A spiritual technique used only as a tool – meditation sold for calm or success alone, “manifesting,” astrology – may draw on something real; but received as one’s own power, cut off from Hashem, it is what he calls “a name of impurity.” The Taz says the same of all wisdom given to the nations: once given, it has “no more attachment to the Giver” (see Part V). The Zohar warns that the books of the East turn a person away from the service of Hashem (see Part III).

When Eastern meditation movements spread among Jews in the 1970s, the Lubavitcher Rebbe called them “cults bordering on, and in some respects actual, Avodah Zarah” (memo, Teves 5738). In a talk in 1979 he pointed to the “burning incense and bowing to a Guru” that came with them, and asked doctors and psychologists to develop a kosher form built on Torah ideas (translated on the Kavvanah blog). Whether a particular practice is permitted is a question for a rav.
Beis Yaakov 33 gives a second reading (
there was no light at all,
because they were born to Avraham
that is, since there was no holiness in them,
a name of impurity was in them.

In 33:2 he adds why Avraham fathered them at all: these nations were fit to be born from Yitzchak, but from his gevurah they would have oppressed Israel. Born from Avraham’s chesed, the opposite of gevurah, the nations oppose one another, and Israel has respite between them (Zohar, Mishpatim 95a).

The Beis Yaakov continues with the Zohar (Vayechi 241b): the “sign of truth” is the letter vav, “for life dwells in it.” The vav is connection; one who lacks it is cut off from the source. So Efron is written with a vav while he was still weighing whether to sell the holy place, and without it (⁧עֶפְרֹן⁩ , 23:16) once he chose the money.
In kabbalah, the Recanati reads the two gifts of these pesukim as the two sides of Avraham’s power (

that Avraham our father, peace be upon him,

the shells of the supernal tree.
he handed to the sons of the concubines…,

מַאי מַתָּנוֹת? אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁמָּסַר לָהֶם שֵׁם טוּמְאָה.

וְהוּא קָשֶׁה לוֹמַר שֶׁיִּמְסוֹר לָהֶם אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֵׁם טוּמְאָה לַעֲשׂוֹת כִּישׁוּף, שֶׁנֶּאֱסַר גַּם לִבְנֵי נֹחַ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּגְּמָרָא (סַנְהֶדְרִין נו:)! וְהָעִיקָּר כְּגִירְסַת הַ"פַּעֲנֵחַ רָזָא" (וְרַשִּׁ"י בַּחוּמָשׁ): "שֶׁמָּסַר לָהֶם שֵׁם בְּטוּמְאָה", וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיָּדַע אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ טְהוֹרִים, וּמָסַר לָהֶם שֵׁם שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לְהַזְכִּירוֹ אַף בְּטוּמְאָה, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בָּהֶם אֵיזֶה שׁוֹרֶשׁ קְדוּשָּׁה שֶׁיִּשָּׁאֵר מֵהֶם אַף לֶעָתִיד שֶׁיִּהְיוּ גֵּרִים גְּרוּרִים.

וְלִבְנֵי הַפִּילַגְשִׁים אֲשֶׁר לְאַבְרָהָם נָתַן אַבְרָהָם מַתְּנֹת וְגוֹמֵר. אָמְרוּ עַל זֶה בְּשִׁשָּׁה סְדָרִים (סַנְהֶדְרִין צא.): שֵׁם טוּמְאָה מָסַר לָהֶם. וְהָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה הוּא, שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵין דְּבַר טוּמְאָה יוֹרֵד מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם, וְהַחִילּוּק הוּא מִצַּד הַמְקַבֵּל הַטּוֹבָה וְהַשְׁפָּעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ. מִי שֶׁמַּכִּיר בְּקַבָּלַת שִׁפְעַת טוֹבָה שֶׁלֹּא בְּכֹחוֹ וְעוֹצֶם יָדוֹ עָשָׂה לוֹ חָיִל, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הַנּוֹתֵן בּוֹ כֹּחַ וְשִׁפְעַת טוֹבָה, זוֹ הִיא טוֹבָה מְלֵאָה קְדוּשָּׁה, וְהַמְקַבְּלָהּ הוּא בֶּן חוֹרִין בְּקַבָּלַת הַטּוֹבָה, מֵאַחַר שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁמִּצִּדּוֹ אֵין לוֹ שׁוּם כֹּחַ, מִמֵּילָא אֵינֶנּוּ מְשׁוּקָּע וְכָפוּף בָּהּ. … וְהָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה הוּא, שֶׁמִּי שֶׁנִּדְמֶה לוֹ שֶׁבְּכֹחוֹ וְעוֹצֶם יָדוֹ עָשָׂה לוֹ חָיִל, אָזַי הוּא כָּפוּף וּמְשׁוּקָּע בְּהַטּוֹבָה, וְכַאֲשֶׁר יְקַבְּלָהּ הוּא עָרִיק מִקַּמֵּי מָארֵיהּ, זֶה נִקְרָא שֵׁם טוּמְאָה. וְלָזֶה כְּתִיב כָּאן מַתְּנֹת חָסֵר ו׳, רָזָא דְּאוֹת אֱמֶת, כִּי אוֹת ו׳ מוֹרֶה עַל חַיִּים שֶׁל אֱמֶת מֵהַמָּקוֹר. … וַיְשַׁלְּחֵם מֵעַל יִצְחָק בְּנוֹ בְּעוֹדֶנּוּ חַי קֵדְמָה אֶל אֶרֶץ קֶדֶם. הַיְינוּ אַף שֶׁהָיוּ זֶה אֵצֶל זֶה, אֲבָל הַפֵּירוּד וְהַחִילּוּק שֶׁבֵּינֵיהֶם הוּא כִּרְחוֹק מִזְרָח מִמַּעֲרָב.
en: Avraham gave all that he had to Yitzchak. And to the sons of the concubines that Avraham had, Avraham gave gifts; and he sent them away from Yitzchak his son while he was still alive, eastward, to the land of the East.
What were the “gifts”? Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba said: This teaches that he handed over to them a name of impurity.
The Gemara’s answer seems to make the question harder. Would Avraham hand his sons a name of impurity?

Now it is difficult to say that Avraham our father would hand them, peace be upon him, a name of impurity to practice sorcery, which is forbidden even to the sons of Noach, as written in the Gemara (Sanhedrin 56b)! Rather, the main reading follows the version of the Pa’aneach Raza (and Rashi on the Chumash): “that he handed them a Name in impurity”; meaning that Avraham our father knew that they would not be pure, and he handed them a Name that they could invoke even in impurity; so that there would be in them some root of holiness that would remain from them even in the future, so that there would be gerim gerurim, converts who come of themselves.

So the gift was holy. Avraham knew where his sons were going, and he gave them a Name that would still work there, so that something of Avraham would survive in them. The Beis Yaakov reads the same words from the side of the one who receives.

“And to the sons of the concubines that Avraham had, Avraham gave gifts,” and so on. On this they said in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 91a): “He handed them a name of impurity.” The meaning is that in truth, from Hashem’s side, nothing impure comes down from heaven; the difference lies with the one who receives the good and the bounty of Hashem. One who recognizes, in receiving abundant good, that not his strength and the might of his hand made him this wealth, but Hashem is the One who gives him strength and abundant good – this is good filled with holiness; and the one who receives it is free in receiving the good, since he recognizes that on his own he has no power; so of itself he is neither sunk in it nor bound to it. … The meaning is that one who imagines that his strength and the might of his hand made him this wealth is then bound to and sunk in the good; and when he receives it, he is running from his Master – this is called a name of impurity. That is why it is written here “matanos” without a vav, the secret of the sign of truth; for the letter vav shows true life from the source. … “He sent them away from Yitzchak his son while he was still alive, eastward, to the land of the East.” That is: even though they were near one another, the separation and difference between them is as far as east is from west.

The two readings agree that the gift came from Hashem through Avraham. Pri Tzaddik speaks of what Avraham planted in his sons. Beis Yaakov speaks of the one who receives it: a gift received as one’s own achievement becomes a “name of impurity.” Both end with the same distance, east of Yitzchak. The next question is what was waiting in the East.

rich.text: What was “the wisdom of the Bnei Kedem”? Rashi on this pasuk (
What is the wisdom of the Bnei Kedem?
They knew the constellations, and so on,
“for they are filled from the East.”
And in the words of our Sages,
What was the wisdom of the Bnei Kedem?
that is, in the language of birds…

The pasuk the Radak cites (Yeshayahu 2:6) goes on: “and soothsayers like the Philistines.” The wisdom of the East, then, was astrology and the reading of omens: real knowledge of how forces from above flow into the world, used to foresee and to control what happens. This is what Rav Tzadok calls the wisdom of idolatry, “drawing down influx and kinds of sorcery” (Likkutei Maamarim, quoted two notes below), and it is the opposite of Avraham, who lived above the stars (“Go out from your astrology,” Shabbos 156a).

Once Shlomo wrote Mishlei, clarifying the wisdom of the Torah, it was no longer needed, “and each thing returned to its proper place.”
Rav Tzadok develops this in Likkutei Maamarim (
and this is the wisdom of the Bnei Kedem,

except the wisdom that wells up

That is the sense of “he was wiser than all men… than all the Bnei Kedem”: ⁧שֶׁנִּיכָּר יִתְרוֹן⁩
of the one over the other.
The Zohar there describes what this wisdom looked like. Rabbi Abba said (

so that your hearts not turn aside

and the inheritance of this wisdom

He knew real things about how blessing flows, and he learned them by divination, not by serving Hashem.
Bilam is the clearest case of this wisdom: real spiritual power, offered for hire. The Torah calls him⁧וְיֹדֵעַ דַּעַת עֶלְיוֹן⁩

Keturah’s son had gone east, and now his descendants bought the power of the East and turned it against the children of Yitzchak. This is the “Da’as of the kelipah”: knowledge of the Most High with no attachment to Him.

: the Sages wished to count Shlomo among those who lose their share in the World to Come, and Bilam, master of the wisdom of the East, was counted in his place, “for of King Solomon it is said: his wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the children of the East.”

Where is this wisdom today? Rav Tzadok and the Izhbitz writers do not say. Several contemporary teachers identify Avraham’s gifts with the religions of the Far East and their meditative disciplines. Rav Pinchas Winston writes that Keturah’s sons “learned to meditate and to create a high level of spiritual sensitivity,” which he takes to be the basis of most Eastern religions; R’ Dov Ber Cohen points to Hindu figures whose names resemble Avraham and Sarah (both cited in Aish, “Abraham’s Impure Gifts to His Children”).

These are modern suggestions, not traditional teachings, and the popular claim that the Hindus descend from Keturah’s sons has no classical source. The Bnei Kedem of Tanach lived much closer, in the Arabian and Syrian deserts (see the note on Bereishis 25:6 in Part II); the identification rests on the character of the wisdom, not on the map. And on that the classical sources are clear: it is spiritual power drawn down by technique and intention (the Zohar’s book of the East, above in this part), close enough to Torah to be confused with it, and for that reason to be kept at a distance.
The Me’or Einayim (Chernobyl) explains “shem tumah” as Torah that fell among the nations, which only the seed of Yitzchak can lift out (

the words that are called a “Name” –

that they have a hold in holiness.
He adds that this is why Yaakov “went to the land of the Bnei Kedem” (Bereishis 29:1), where Avraham had sent the sons of the concubines: to lift those fallen words back to their root.

Pri Tzaddik’s proof: the Gemara (Sanhedrin 59b) includes the sons of Keturah in the mitzvah of milah, and the Rambam (Hilchos Melachim 10:8) rules that their descendants, now mixed with Yishmael, are obligated in every generation. The servants circumcised with Avraham, by contrast, left the covenant after his death (Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 29).

וּקְטוּרָה, אַף שֶׁהָיְתָה צְנוּעָה בְּמַעֲשֶׂיהָ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ ("שֶׁנָּאִים מַעֲשֶׂיהָ כִּקְטֹרֶת"), מִכָּל מָקוֹם שָׁרְשָׁהּ הָיָה מִקְּלִיפַּת מִצְרַיִם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: "זוֹ הָגָר", שֶׁהָיְתָה שִׁפְחָה מִצְרִית; וְזַרְעָהּ שִׁילַּח אַבְרָהָם אֶל אֶרֶץ קֶדֶם וּמָסַר לָהֶם שֵׁם בְּטוּמְאָה – דְּאַף שֶׁהֵם בְּטוּמְאָה יִהְיֶה בָּהֶן שׁוֹרֶשׁ קְדוּשָּׁה, וּמֵהֶם יוֹצִיאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל הַחַיּוּת וְהַנִּיצוֹצוֹת הַקְּדוֹשִׁים דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, וּמֵהֶם יִשָּׁאֵר גֵּרִים גְּרוּרִין לֶעָתִיד. … וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶם שׁוֹרֶשׁ קְדוּשָּׁה יוֹתֵר מִבְּנֵי עֵשָׂו שֶׁפְּטוּרִין מִמִּילָה!

וְזֶה הַמְּכֻוָּון בְּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה סא, ז): "וַיְשַׁלְּחֵם מֵעַל יִצְחָק בְּנוֹ... קֵדְמָה אֶל אֶרֶץ קֶדֶם" – אָמַר לָהֶם: כָּל מַה שֶּׁאַתֶּם יְכוֹלִים לְהַזְרִיחַ תַּזְרִיחוּ, שֶׁלֹּא תִּכָּווּ בְּגַחַלְתּוֹ שֶׁל יִצְחָק. וְלִפְשׁוּטוֹ דְּקָאֵי עַל רוּחַ מִזְרָח, אֵינוֹ מְדוּקְדָּק לְשׁוֹן "לְהַזְרִיחַ תַּזְרִיחוּ"; אַךְ הַמְּכֻוָּון: "לְהַזְרִיחַ" – לְהוֹפִיעַ אוֹר, "תַּזְרִיחוּ" – תָּאִירוּ אוֹר מֵהַשֵּׁם שֶׁמָּסַר לָהֶם, וְהוּא כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּשָּׁאֵר מֵהֶם הַשְׁאָרָה לִהְיוֹת גֵּרִים גְּרוּרִים; וְאָמַר "שֶׁלֹּא תִּכָּווּ בְּגַחַלְתּוֹ שֶׁל יִצְחָק" – הַיְינוּ אֵשׁ דִּקְדוּשָּׁה שֶׁהוּא תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית ד.): "הַאי צוּרְבָא מֵרַבָּנָן דְּרָתַח, אוֹרַיְיתָא הִיא דְּקָא מְרַתְּחָא לֵיהּ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: הֲלוֹא כֹה דְבָרִי כָּאֵשׁ (יִרְמְיָה כג, כט)"; וּ"דְבָרִי" הַיְינוּ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וָאָשִׂם דְּבָרַי בְּפִיךָ" (יְשַׁעְיָה נא, טז); וְכֵן כָּתוּב בְּהַקְדָּמַת תִּקּוּנֵי זֹהַר: "וְכַד אִתְנְטִילַת מִגְּבוּרָה (מִדַּת יִצְחָק) אִתְקְרִיאַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה וְכוּלֵי".
en: Now it is written: “Shlomo’s wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the Bnei Kedem and all the wisdom of Egypt” (I Melachim 5:10). This is as it is written: “And You give life to them all” (Nechemiah 9:6); and the essence of life is words of Torah. In Egypt there was in exile all of the Written Torah, and of this it is said: “And afterwards they will go out with great wealth” (Bereishis 15:14) – that is, when they draw out of them all the vitality and holiness; for they made it like a trap with no grain in it, and like a deep with no fish in it, as they said (Berachos 9b) – that is, all of life: this is what “fish” hints at, for of them the Torah first uses the term “living soul” (Bereishis 1:20), for in them is the root of life; and “grain” is what sustains life. Through this they merited the giving of the Torah, and that is the “great wealth.” And in “the wisdom of all the Bnei Kedem” – there was in exile the Oral Torah; and they are in the kelipah, “one opposite the other,” facing the Oral Torah. As it says in the holy Zohar (end of this parsha, 133b): “For in those mountains of the East are those who teach sorcery to mankind, and from that land of the East came Lavan and Be’or and Bilam his son” – see there. And Bilam was the Da’as of the kelipah, as written in the holy Zohar (III 194a). Of this the pasuk says that “the wisdom of Shlomo” – which is the Lower Wisdom, the Oral Torah – “excelled” (it grew from his drawing out the holy sparks) “beyond the wisdom of all the Bnei Kedem and all the wisdom of Egypt.” And though the wisdom of Egypt was in the kelipah opposite the Written Torah, it mentions the wisdom of Egypt too, because the Oral Torah has its root in the Written Torah.
Now Keturah herself enters the picture. She is Hagar, and her root is in Egypt; her children were sent to the East. Between them, mother and sons touch both exiled wisdoms.

And Keturah, though she was modest in her deeds, as they said in the Midrash (“her deeds were as pleasing as incense”) – nevertheless her root was from the kelipah of Egypt, as they said there: “This is Hagar,” who was an Egyptian maidservant. And her offspring Avraham sent to the land of the East, and handed them a Name in impurity – so that even while they are in impurity there would be in them a root of holiness; and from them Israel would draw out the vitality and the holy sparks of the Oral Torah; and from them would remain gerim gerurim in the future. … Perforce, there is in them a root of holiness more than in the sons of Esav, who are exempt from milah!

And this is the meaning of what they said in Midrash Rabbah (61:7): “He sent them away from Yitzchak his son… eastward, to the land of the East” – he said to them: As far east as you can go (lehazriach, “to shine”), go east (tazrichu), so that you are not burned by the coal of Yitzchak. By its plain sense, referring to the eastern direction, the wording is not precise: “lehazriach tazrichu” – to cause to shine. Rather, the meaning is: “lehazriach” – to make light appear; “tazrichu” – shine light from the Name he handed them; so that there would remain a remnant of them to become gerim gerurim. And he said, “so that you are not burned by the coal of Yitzchak” – meaning the fire of holiness, which is the Oral Torah, as they said (Taanis 4a): “A young Torah scholar who grows heated – it is the Torah that heats him, as it says: ‘Is not My word like fire?’ (Yirmiyah 23:29).” And “My word” is the Oral Torah, as it says: “I have put My words in your mouth” (Yeshayah 51:16); and so it is written in the Introduction to Tikkunei Zohar: “And when it is taken from Gevurah (the attribute of Yitzchak), it is called the Oral Torah,” and so on.

Avraham sent his sons away to protect them. Close to Yitzchak, the fire of the Oral Torah would have burned them. Far away, they could shine whatever light the Name gave them, and that light would one day bring some of them back as converts.

he: אַךְ הָעִנְיָן עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא (זְבָחִים סב:): "קָרֵי עֲלַיְיהוּ: בְּנֵי קְטוּרָה!" וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י: בְּנֵי אַבְרָהָם אַתֶּם, אֲבָל לֹא כְּזֶרַע יִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב. וְאַחַר כָּךְ אִיתָא שָׁם: "בְּנֵי אֲחָתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי טַרְפוֹן הֲווֹ יָתְבֵי קַמֵּיהּ... פָּתַח וְאָמַר: וַיֹּסֶף אַבְרָהָם וַיִּקַּח אִשָּׁה וּשְׁמָהּ יוֹחָנִי. אָמְרוּ לֵיהּ: קְטוּרָה כְּתִיב! קָרֵי עֲלַיְיהוּ: בְּנֵי קְטוּרָה!" וְיֵשׁ לְהָבִין: וְכִי מִפְּנֵי שֶׁלֹּא יָדְעוּ בַּהֲלָכָה קָרוּ לְהוּ "בְּנֵי קְטוּרָה"? גַּם בַּמַּהֲרְשָׁ"א הִקְשָׁה: לָמָּה לֹא קְרָאָם "בְּנֵי עֵשָׂו", שֶׁאַף שֶׁהֵם בְּנֵי אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, אֵינָם בְּנֵי יַעֲקֹב?

וְזֶה הָעִנְיָן שֶׁקָּרָא רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן לְהָנְהוּ דְּמַחֲכוּ עֲלֵיהּ וְלֹא הֵבִינוּ כַּוָּנָתוֹ: "בְּנֵי קְטוּרָה!" (וְלֹא בְּנֵי עֵשָׂו) – דִּכְמוֹ בִּבְנֵי קְטוּרָה שֶׁהָיָה בְּשָׁרְשָׁם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, רַק הֵם לֹא זָכוּ לָזֶה, וּשְׁלֹמֹה הוֹצִיא מֵהֶם הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה – כֵּן גַּם בָּכֶם יֵשׁ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְלֹא זְכִיתֶם לְהָבִין! … וְהֵם לֹא הֵבִינוּ אֶת כַּוָּנָתוֹ וְאָמְרוּ לֵיהּ כִּפְשׁוּטוֹ: "קְטוּרָה כְּתִיב!" וְלָכֵן קָרֵי עֲלַיְיהוּ "בְּנֵי קְטוּרָה!", שֶׁלֹּא הֵבִינוּ עוֹמֶק כַּוָּנָתוֹ בְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.
en: But the matter is according to what they said in the Gemara (Zevachim 62b): “He applied to them: ‘Sons of Keturah!’” And Rashi explains: You are sons of Avraham, but not like the seed of Yitzchak and Yaakov. And afterwards it says there: “The sons of Rabbi Tarfon’s sister were sitting before him… He opened and said: ‘And Avraham again took a wife, and her name was Yochani.’ They said to him: ‘Keturah is written!’ He applied to them: ‘Sons of Keturah!’” We must understand: just because they did not know the halachah, did he call them “sons of Keturah”? The Maharsha also asks: why did he not call them “sons of Esav,” who, though they are sons of Avraham and Yitzchak, are not sons of Yaakov?

And this is why Rabbi Tarfon called those who laughed at him and did not understand his intent: “Sons of Keturah!” (and not “sons of Esav”) – for just as with the sons of Keturah, in whose root there were words of Torah of the Oral Torah, only they did not merit it, and Shlomo drew out of them the Oral Torah – so too in you there are words of Torah, and you have not merited to understand! … And they did not understand his intent, and said to him plainly: “Keturah is written!” So he applied to them: “Sons of Keturah!” for they did not grasp the depth of his intent in the Oral Torah.

Rabbi Tarfon did not call them sons of Esav, because his point was not that they lacked Torah. A son of Keturah carries the sparks of the Oral Torah and cannot read them. His nephews knew the pasuk and missed the hint. The rebuke fits anyone who holds the words of Torah and misses their depth.

וְאֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדוֹת יִשְׁמָעֵאל בֶּן אַבְרָהָם וְגוֹמֵר. הָעִנְיָן שֶׁיִּשְׁמָעֵאל נִקְרָא בֶּן אַבְרָהָם יוֹתֵר מֵהָאוּמּוֹת שֶׁהוֹלִיד אַחַר כָּךְ, לְפִי שֶׁבְּלֵידַת יִשְׁמָעֵאל הָיְתָה הָגָר אִמּוֹ שִׁפְחַת שָׂרָה עוֹד, שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נִשְׁלַם עוֹד בְּכָל הַשְּׁלֵימוּת; לָזֶה הָיָה בּוֹ מְעַט קְדוּשָּׁה. כִּי הָאָדָם קוֹדֶם הַשְׁלָמָתוֹ הוּא נִכְנָס לְכָל הַסְּפֵיקוֹת פֶּן יַרְוִיחַ מִזֶּה. אֲבָל הַתּוֹלָדוֹת שֶׁהוֹלִיד אַחַר זֶה, שֶׁמֵּתָה שָׂרָה וְהָיָה נִשְׁלַם בְּכָל הַשְּׁלֵימוּת וְלֹא הָיָה צָרִיךְ לְשׁוּם עֲבוֹדָה כְּלָל – … לָזֶה לֹא הָיָה בְּאֵלֶּה הַתּוֹלָדוֹת שׁוּם קְדוּשָּׁה וְכֹחַ בִּפְנִימִיּוּת. וְלָזֶה גֵּרֵי יִשְׁמָעֵאל הֵם גְּדוֹלִים בְּמַעֲלָה מִגֵּרֵי שְׁאָר הָאוּמּוֹת, כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (יִתְרוֹ פז.).
en: The parsha closes with a second family outside Avraham’s house. Yishmael’s wisdom is of another kind: not hidden Torah, but the wisdom of the natural world. The Izhbitzer reads it straight out of the names of his sons.

“These are the generations of Yishmael, son of Avraham, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s maidservant, bore to Avraham.” It is written (Tehillim 111:6): “The power of His works He told His people, to give them the heritage of the nations” – meaning that for Israel, on their own side, there is no need for them to know any wisdom of nature; for by the Torah of Hashem and Hashem’s conduct of the world they conduct themselves, with no need at all for the ways of nature – only “He Who told the oil to burn will tell the vinegar to burn” (Taanis 25a). Yet Hashem, out of His love for them, wanted to let them know the wisdoms of nature too, and this too is found in the Torah, as we find in the Gemara (Pesachim 39b): “A person may not chew wheat on Pesach to put on his wound” – from which we learn, in passing, that chewed wheat is good for a wound; and so we find in several places. And so “the power of His works” – that is, the Torah – “He told His people, to give them the heritage of the nations”; for their heritage is nature, and this too is found in “the power of His works” that He told His people. And this is “These are the generations of Yishmael… Sarah’s maidservant, to Avraham”: for his main lineage is that she was Sarah’s maidservant, and because of this there are wise men among them. For their names show their wisdom. Nevayos teaches that a person must see to it that his body is kept clean – from the word navuv, hollow; and Kedar is a body kept warm; and Adbe’el – that one should not eat to full satiety; and Mivsam (fragrance) – “wine and fragrances make one sharp” (Yoma 76b). This is their wisdom in matters of bodily health. And their wisdom between man and his fellow is Mishma, Dumah and Massa: to listen, to be silent, and to bear with others. And their wisdom for what lies ahead: Chadad – if you want to do something new (chadash), and Teima – so that the whole world will marvel (temah) at it; Yetur – see to it that it is well set in order (tur); Nafish – to rest and settle well into the thing; and Kedmah – if you see that it is right, be first (takdim) to do it, lest others get ahead of you. But all their wisdom is only in matters of nature, and in this they put their trust; and so it is written of him: “Before all his brothers he fell,” while of Israel, who know that everything is from Heaven, it is written “he shall dwell.”

[And this is what the Gemara says (Berachos 58a): One who sees the sages of Israel says: “Blessed is He Who apportioned (chalak) of His wisdom to those who fear Him”; on the sages of the nations he says: “Blessed is He Who gave (nasan) of His wisdom to flesh and blood.” The same difference holds between the kings of Israel and the kings of the nations. This is because Israel are a portion (chelek) of Him, while the wisdom of the nations is the wisdom of nature and has no connection to holiness; for the wisdom and conduct of Israel are by the Torah of Hashem. End of addendum.]

The Izhbitzer does not dismiss this wisdom. Hashem placed it in the Torah “out of His love,” and Yishmael has it because his mother was Sarah’s maidservant. The Beis Yaakov, the Izhbitzer’s son, reads the same pasuk and the same words, “shifchas Sarah,” as the measure of holiness in Yishmael.

“These are the generations of Yishmael, son of Avraham,” and so on. The point is that Yishmael is called Avraham’s son more than the nations that he fathered later, because at Yishmael’s birth Hagar his mother was still Sarah’s maidservant, when Avraham our father, peace be upon him, had not yet reached full completion; therefore there was in him a little holiness. For a person, before he is complete, enters every uncertain venture in case he may gain from it. But the offspring that he fathered afterwards, when Sarah had died and he was fully complete and no longer needed any service at all – … therefore there was not, in these offspring, any holiness or inner power. And so converts from Yishmael are greater in standing than converts from the other nations, as the holy Zohar says (Yisro 87a).

The Beis Yaakov and Pri Tzaddik weigh Keturah’s sons differently, and the difference is instructive. The Beis Yaakov speaks of what was in them from birth: born after Avraham’s completion, they had no inner holiness. Pri Tzaddik speaks of what Avraham gave them afterwards: a Name that keeps a root of holiness alive in them, even in impurity.

en: Mei HaShiloach said that Yishmael fell because he trusted his wisdom of nature. The Beis Yaakov takes the next step: wisdom that is not attached to Hashem is worth nothing, however useful it is.

“Before all his brothers he fell.” First it says “he shall dwell,” and afterwards it says “he fell.” This is as they said in the holy Zohar (Yisro 86a): “He will be a wild man” – “a wild man, and not a man. A wild man, because he was circumcised, and the beginning of a man was in him and so on; but he was not completed by the mitzvos of the Torah. But the seed of Israel, who were completed in everything, are called truly ‘man.’” That is: though he had the wisdom of how to guard the body, which helps toward ruach hakodesh, as the Talmud says (Nedarim 38a): “The Holy One, blessed be He, rests His Shechinah only on one who is wise, strong and wealthy” – still, one who does not cleave to Hashem – then there is no worth at all in these wisdoms. That is why it is written of him: “Before all his brothers he fell”; for the main thing is to cleave to Hashem. For one who cleaves to Hashem – there pursue him all good things, of themselves, as it says in the Talmud (Yoma 18a): “The kohen who is greater than his brothers” – make him great from what is his brothers’.

Father and son read “nafal” the same way from two sides. For the Izhbitzer, Yishmael fell because he trusted nature. For the Beis Yaakov, the wisdom of the body is real, and even helps bring ruach hakodesh, but without attachment it has no weight. The one who cleaves to Hashem does not need to chase it; it comes to him.

דְּמָשְׁלוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה כְּשָׁפִים לְתֶבֶן, וְכֵן הִמְשִׁיל הַכָּתוּב נְבוּאַת שֶׁקֶר נֶגֶד נְבוּאַת אֱמֶת: "מַה לַתֶּבֶן אֶת הַבָּר" (יִרְמְיָה כג, כח). … וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהַתֶּבֶן נוֹשֵׂא הַבָּר כָּל זְמַן הַגִּידּוּל, כֵּן הַשֶּׁקֶר נוֹשֵׂא לִנְבוּאַת הָאֱמֶת. … אֲבָל אַחַר שֶׁגָּדַל הַבָּר – הַתֶּבֶן נִזְרָק; וְכֵן בְּהַשְׁלָמַת יִצְחָק וּמִדָּתוֹ – אָז: "וַיֹּסֶף וְגוֹמֵר... וַיְשַׁלְּחֵם".

וּמִי הוּא שֶׁיָּכוֹל לְהַרְאוֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּכָל בְּרִיאָה כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם, אֲפִילּוּ בְּהַדּוֹמֵם? וְזֶה הוּא יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ, שֶׁהוּא יָכוֹל "יַשְׁמִיעַ כָּל תְּהִלָּתוֹ"; שֶׁהַשְּׁנֵים עָשָׂר שְׁבָטִים שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב הָיוּ יוֹצְאִין מִתְּחִלָּה מִנָּחוֹר וְאַחַר כָּךְ מִיִּשְׁמָעֵאל, וְלֹא הָיָה רַק לְתַתָּא, הַיְינוּ בְּיִשּׁוּב הַדַּעַת שֶׁל עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כִּדְאִיתָא בְּמֵי הַשִּׁילֹחַ (חֵלֶק א, סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת חַיֵּי שָׂרָה, דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "וְאֵלֶּה") שֶׁזֶּה מוֹרִים הַשֵּׁמוֹת שֶׁל בְּנֵי יִשְׁמָעֵאל. וְעַכְשָׁיו יוֹצְאִין אֵלּוּ הַנְּפָשׁוֹת בְּעַצְמָן עַל יְדֵי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ בִּשְׁנֵים עָשָׂר שְׁבָטִים, וְאֵלּוּ הֵם לְעֵילָּא, שֶׁהֵם מְלֵאִים דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁהֵם קַיָּימִים לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים; מוֹסִיף שֶׁבַח עַל הָרִאשׁוֹנִים, שֶׁהֵם לֹא הָיוּ רַק מָשָׁל וְדִמְיוֹן, שֶׁהָיוּ צְרִיכִים לֵילֵךְ דֶּרֶךְ יַעֲקֹב; כִּי אֲפִילּוּ מִיִּשְׁמָעֵאל, שֶׁהוּא חָבִיב מִכָּל הָאֻמּוֹת, אִם יִרְצֶה לְהִדָּבֵק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, מוּכְרָח לֵילֵךְ דֶּרֶךְ יַעֲקֹב, שֶׁיְּעוֹרֵר בּוֹ חַיִּים; כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִבְטִיחַ לְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם (בְּרֵאשִׁית כב, יז): "וְיִרַשׁ זַרְעֲךָ אֵת שַׁעַר אֹיְבָיו", וְהַשַּׁעַר הוּא יַעֲקֹב, שֶׁעַל יָדוֹ יְכוֹלִים לִכָּנֵס לִקְדֻשָּׁה, וּבְלֹא דֶּרֶךְ יַעֲקֹב אֵין לָהֶם שַׁעַר כְּלָל; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהֵם עוֹמְדִים בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָן, אַף שֶׁיִּרְצוּ לַעֲבוֹד אֶת הַשֵּׁם, לֹא יָאִיר לָהֶם רַק כְּשֶׁיִּכָּנְסוּ דֶּרֶךְ יַעֲקֹב. לָכֵן כְּתִיב "וְאֵלֶּה".
en: If the wisdom outside the house is a husk, why did it come first? Yishmael had twelve princes before Yaakov had twelve tribes. Three passages answer from three sides.

“Twelve princes for their nations.” The point is that Yishmael had twelve princes matching the twelve princes of holiness; for the husk always comes before the fruit. So there came first the twelve princes of Yishmael, who are the husk; and it is for the good of the fruit, so that it will be good for Israel. So too from the beginning of creation Hashem prepared all the good things for man, so that it would be good for him.

For the Sages compared sorcery to straw, and so the pasuk compares false prophecy to true prophecy: “What is the straw to the grain?” (Yirmiyah 23:28). … And just as the straw carries the grain all the while it grows, so falsehood carries the prophecy of truth. … But once the grain has grown, the straw is thrown away; and so, when Yitzchak and his attribute were complete – then: “And he again… and he sent them away.”

And who is able to show that in every creature there is the glory of Heaven, even in the inanimate? That is Yaakov our father, who is able to “declare all His praise.” For the twelve tribes of Yaakov were coming out at first from Nachor, and afterwards from Yishmael; but it was only below, that is, in the practical understanding of this world, as it says in Mei HaShiloach (Part I, end of Chayei Sarah, s.v. “Ve’eileh”), that this is what the names of Yishmael’s sons show. And now there come out these very same souls through Yaakov our father, in the twelve tribes; and these are above, for they are full of words of Torah that endure forever and ever. It adds praise over the first ones, who were nothing but a parable and likeness, who had to go by way of Yaakov. For even from Yishmael, the dearest of all the nations, one who wants to cleave to Hashem must go by way of Yaakov, who will awaken life in him. For Hashem promised Avraham our father, peace be upon him, (Bereishis 22:17): “Your seed will inherit the gate of his enemies”; and the gate is Yaakov, through whom one can enter holiness; and without the way of Yaakov they have no gate at all. As they are, standing on their own, even if they want to serve Hashem, He will not shine for them, only when they enter by way of Yaakov. That is why it is written “Ve’eileh.”

The three passages fit together. The husk comes first and protects the fruit (Beis Yaakov 39). The chaff carries the grain while it grows and is thrown away once Yitzchak is complete (Kometz HaMinchah). And what Yishmael’s sons held “below,” as wisdom for this world, comes out again in Yaakov’s twelve tribes “above,” full of Torah (Beis Yaakov, Toldos 7). Even for Yishmael, the way back into holiness is through Yaakov.

Three sources, one picture. Yishmael returned in Avraham’s merit (Pri Tzaddik 8). He returned because the root of Avraham in him would not let him stay as he was, though his teshuvah could not erase the past as Israel’s does (Divrei Soferim). And he could return at all because his side, desire, the chesed of the kelipah, can be refined into holiness, while Esav’s cannot (Pri Tzaddik, Mishpatim).

“Dross” is the scum and slag that separates out when silver or gold is melted down and refined, and is skimmed off and thrown away. The Hebrew is ⁧סִיגִים⁩  (sigim), as in
Remove the dross from the silver,
and a vessel comes out for the smith.

Divrei Soferim’s own word is ⁧פְּסֹלֶת⁩  (p’soles), “refuse”: what is left over and rejected once the good has been taken. The image matters for the argument. Dross comes out of the same ore as the precious metal and still carries something of it; that is why Yishmael, Avraham’s dross, still has “the root of Avraham” in him. And dross is what must be removed for the vessel to be made: Yishmael and Keturah’s sons were separated out so that Yitzchak and Yaakov could come out pure.
The Zohar uses the same image. Avraham is silver (chesed) and Yitzchak is gold (gevurah); their other sons are the dross of each (

וְשַׁיָּיכוּת הַפְטָרָה זוֹ לְפָרָשָׁה זוֹ הוּא לֹא רַק לְמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר בָּהּ "וְאַבְרָהָם זָקֵן בָּא בַּיָּמִים", רַק לְכָל הַפָּרָשָׁה כֻּלָּהּ שֶׁמְּדַבֶּרֶת מֵעִנְיָן זֶה (שְׁלֵימוּת הַזִּקְנָה בְּכָל הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת): … וְאַחַר כָּךְ בְּסוֹף הַפָּרָשָׁה כְּתִיב: "וְאֵלֶּה שְׁנֵי חַיֵּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל... וַיִּגְוַע וַיָּמָת וַיֵּאָסֶף אֶל עַמָּיו" (כה, יז) – שֶׁזָּכָה גַּם כֵּן בִּשְׁבִיל אַבְרָהָם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ גְּוִיעָה וַאֲסִיפָה כַּצַּדִּיקִים, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁעָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה בְּחַיֵּי אַבְרָהָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טז:).

en: Yishmael’s story does not end with “he fell.” The Torah has already shown him at his father’s burial, and it describes his death in words used for the righteous.

They buried him, Yitzchak and Yishmael his sons, in the Cave of Machpelah. … These are the years of Yishmael’s life: a hundred and thirty years and seven years; he expired and died, and was gathered to his people.
The Gemara has said that a death described with both “expiring” and “being gathered” is the death of the righteous. It asks:

But what about Yishmael, of whom it is written “expiring” and “being gathered”! Meanwhile Rava woke up and said to them: Children, this is what Rabbi Yochanan said: Yishmael did teshuvah in his father’s lifetime, as it says: “They buried him, Yitzchak and Yishmael his sons.”

The connection of this haftarah to this parsha is not only to what is said in it, “And Avraham was old, advanced in days,” but to the whole parsha, which speaks of this theme: (the completeness of old age at every level). … And then, at the end of the parsha, it is written: “These are the years of Yishmael’s life… he expired and died, and was gathered to his people” (25:17) – for he too merited, because of Avraham, that there is said of him “expiring” and “being gathered,” like the righteous, because he did teshuvah in Avraham’s lifetime, as they said (Bava Basra 16b).
Divrei Soferim has just called Esav, Yitzchak’s dross, the root of all actual sin. Yishmael, the dross of Avraham, is different:

But Yishmael did teshuvah, as the Sages said (there, Bava Basra 16b); except that teshuvah does not work for the nations, for teshuvah was given only to Israel, as our early authorities wrote, and it is also found in Tanchuma, Haazinu. Nevertheless: as a gentile, he has no connection to Israel, only insofar as he is the dross of Avraham. In Avraham it was only potential, and its coming into actuality is in Yishmael; for what is potential in the father becomes actual in the son. And the coming into actuality of Avraham’s dross is only in offspring among the nations, which is not called his seed. Therefore even in Yishmael himself, because of the power of Avraham in him, he did not have the strength to stay that way; and in the end, because of the root of Avraham in him, he did teshuvah; except that it did not help him to repair the past as it does in Israel, where after teshuvah the sin no longer exists.

For it is known that there are two kelipos, of right and left, in “one opposite the other”: the dross of chesed and gevurah of holiness. These are the kelipos of Yishmael and Esav, corresponding to the two flaws mentioned above. Yishmael is desire, the flaw of the covenant, the chesed within the kelipah; and Esav is murder, anger and evil speech. … That is, the kelipah of Yishmael can be refined into holiness, and therefore it is said of him that he did teshuvah (as stated in Bava Basra 16b). But the kelipah of Esav has no repair, and must be eradicated completely, as it says: “There will be no survivor of the house of Esav.” For this reason converts are not accepted from Amalek (as stated in the Mechilta, end of Beshalach).

Three sources, one picture. Yishmael returned in Avraham’s merit (Pri Tzaddik 8). He returned because the root of Avraham in him would not let him stay as he was, though his teshuvah could not erase the past as Israel’s does (Divrei Soferim). And he could return at all because his side, desire, the chesed of the kelipah, can be refined into holiness, while Esav’s cannot (Pri Tzaddik, Mishpatim).

en: Now we can return to the question we began with: why does the Midrash call Yitzchak the small beginning, and the sons of Keturah the great increase?

And this is what is expounded in Midrash Tanchuma: “though your beginning was small” – of Yitzchak our father, peace be upon him; “your latter end will greatly increase” – of the sons of Keturah: for from them Israel draws out, in the end, all the depth of the Oral Torah (the light that comes out of the darkness), as it is written: “Shlomo’s wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the Bnei Kedem,” as we have said! And this is why it says “will greatly (me’od) increase” – in the manner of what is said: “God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very (me’od) good” (Bereishis 1:31), which is expounded (Bereishis Rabbah 9) of everything opposed to the good that will be turned into “very good,” and in the manner of what is written (in the holy Zohar II 184a): “There is no light except that which comes out of darkness, and there is no good except that which comes out of evil.” For precisely from this comes “very good,” and that is what it says: “your latter end will greatly increase.” And the pasuk “God saw… and behold, it was very good” was said at the end of the sixth day, at the time of the addition of Shabbos; for Shabbos is the time to merit the Oral Torah, which is the “much wisdom” that repairs the “much vexation,” so that it becomes “very good,” as it is written (Zohar I 47b): “‘On the seventh day’ – this is the Oral Torah, which is the seventh day,” and so on; that is, Malchus, the mouth – the Oral Torah.

phrases: Pri Tzaddik said that from the sons of Keturah “Israel draws out, in the end, all the depth of the Oral Torah.” The end did not come all at once. Israel was sent back to the East, to Bavel, and later spread through all the lands of Yishmael; and out of those lands, generation after generation, came Torah that shone brighter for the darkness around it. First the sources that explain why, and then the people.
The Holy One, blessed be He, exiled
only because it is deep as She’ol,
“From the hand of She’ol I will ransom them,
from death I will redeem them.”
Because He sent them back to their mother’s house.

Bavel is Avraham’s house, the East he came out of. Rabbi Elazar adds why the exile went there: it is “deep as She’ol,” and from that depth Hashem redeems. Rav Tzadok explains what that depth produced.

this is the Talmud of Bavel.
“He has set me in dark places”:
And this too was brought about by
And the light that comes out of darkness

This is the rule behind the whole part. The stronger the darkness of a place, the greater the light that can be drawn out of it, and the Oral Torah in particular grows in the “uglier vessel.” Pri Tzaddik applies it to Bavel first, and then to all the other lands of exile.
these are the exiles of Bavel,
whose minds are settled, like sons;
“and My daughters from the end of the earth” –
these are the exiles of the other lands,
of the Oral Torah was in Bavel,
“Ezra came up from Bavel and established it…;
“He has set me in dark places” –
this is the Talmud of Bavel.

Pri Tzaddik gives the theory both of its parts. Bavel, the East, is the main home of the Oral Torah, drawn out of the darkness. And the “daughters,” the exiles of all the other lands, also “did valiantly.”
This is connected to the well-known tradition

It follows that this power was in Sisera,

The greatest of the Oral Torah was first “outside,” wrapped in a husk, and had to be drawn out of it. Pri Tzaddik traces the same Rabbi Akiva back to Keturah’s own family.
is the root of the Oral Torah,
and he was a son of converts…

which belongs to the Oral Torah…
And it says in Asarah Maamaros
that Rabbi Akiva came from Sisera,
And the Kenites went to Yaabetz
some merited to sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone,
and from there is the root of the Oral Torah.

Yisro was the priest of Midian, and Midian was a son of Keturah. Pri Tzaddik’s promise in Chayei Sarah, that Israel would draw the sparks of the Oral Torah out of Keturah’s sons, is fulfilled in Yisro’s family: the Kenites on the Sanhedrin and, by this tradition, Rabbi Akiva himself. The same pattern continued in every later generation. What follows is our application of these sources to Jewish history; Rav Tzadok does not name these people.

The land Avraham came out of, and where the Talmud was made, went on giving. In nineteenth-century Baghdad, Chacham Abdallah Somech taught a generation of scholars, and his student Rabbi Yosef Chaim, the Ben Ish Chai (1835–1909), became the master of halachah and kabbalah for all of Sephardi Jewry.50Rabbi Yosef Chaim of Baghdad (1835–1909), known by his work Ben Ish Chai, which joins kabbalah with practical halachah and is standard in Sephardi homes; also Ben Yehoyada on the aggados of the Talmud and the responsa Rav Pe’alim. His main teacher was Chacham Abdallah Somech (1813–1889). See Wikipedia: Yosef Hayyim. From his circle came Rabbi Yaakov Chaim Sofer, author of the Kaf HaChaim, born in Baghdad in 1870, and the kabbalist Rabbi Yehuda Fatiyah (1859–1942), the authority of his day on spirits and gilgulim, whose Minchas Yehuda draws on his encounters with them: the work of drawing souls out of the kelipah in its most literal form.51Rabbi Yaakov Chaim Sofer (Baghdad 1870 – Jerusalem 1939), a student of Chacham Abdallah Somech and the Ben Ish Chai, settled in Jerusalem and wrote the Kaf HaChaim (Wikipedia). Rabbi Yehuda Fatiyah (Baghdad 1859 – Jerusalem 1942), the leading student of the Ben Ish Chai, wrote Beis Lechem Yehuda on the Etz Chaim and Minchas Yehuda, and was the recognized authority on amulets, gilgulim and spirits (Wikipedia). In the twentieth century Baghdad’s sons led Torah in Jerusalem: the kabbalists Rabbi Salman Mutzafi (1900–1974) and Rabbi Yitzchak Kaduri (c. 1898–2006), and Rabbi Ovadia Yosef (1920–2013), born in Baghdad and brought to Jerusalem as a child, who restored the honor of Sephardi halachah in our generation.52Rabbi Salman Mutzafi (Baghdad 1900 – Jerusalem 1974) learned under Rabbi Yehuda Fatiyah at Midrash Zilkha and founded a yeshiva for Zohar and kabbalah near Kever Rachel (Daily Zohar). Rabbi Yitzchak Kaduri (Baghdad c. 1898 – Jerusalem 2006) learned with the Ben Ish Chai, Rabbi Fatiyah, the Kaf HaChaim and Rabbi Ezra Attiya, and taught the kavanos of the Rashash (Wikipedia). Rabbi Ovadia Yosef was born in Baghdad in 1920 and brought to Jerusalem as a small child, where he learned at Porat Yosef under Rabbi Ezra Attiya (Aish).

Aleppo is Aram Tzova and Damascus is Aram Dammesek: the land of Lavan and Bilam. For some six hundred years Aleppo’s great synagogue guarded the Keter Aram Tzova, the codex of Tanach that the Rambam relied on, until the riots of 1947.53The codex was written in Tiberias around 920 and vocalized by Aharon ben Asher. The Rambam used it as his authority for the writing of a Sefer Torah. It reached Aleppo by about 1375 and was kept in the Central Synagogue for some five to six centuries; after the synagogue was burned in 1947 it was hidden, and it reached Jerusalem in 1958, missing many pages (Wikipedia: Aleppo Codex). Out of Aleppo came Rabbi Ezra Attiya (1885–1970), for forty-five years rosh yeshiva of Porat Yosef in Jerusalem and the teacher of a generation of Sephardi gedolim.54Born in Aleppo in 1885; mashgiach of Porat Yosef when it opened in 1923 and rosh yeshiva from 1925 until his death in 1970 (Wikipedia: Ezra Attiya). Among his students were Rabbi Yehuda Tzadka, Rabbi Yitzchak Kaduri and Rabbi Ovadia Yosef. And the line of the Baba Sali begins in Damascus: the family’s patriarch, Rabbi Shmuel Elbaz (Abuchatzeira), lived there and learned with Rabbi Chaim Vital before his descendants settled in Morocco.55The patriarch of the Abuchatzeira family, Rabbi Shmuel Elbaz, was born in Eretz Yisrael, lived for a time in Damascus and learned Torah with Rabbi Chaim Vital; the Chida called him “a holy man of God.” His descendants settled in Rissani, Morocco (Wikipedia: Baba Sali).

Charan, where Avraham lived and where Yaakov found Rachel and Leah, lies in today’s Turkey. Under the Ottomans, Turkey became a home of Torah. Rabbi Yosef Karo began the Beis Yosef in Adrianople (Edirne); Rabbi Yaakov Culi (1689–1732) began the Me’am Lo’ez in Constantinople, bringing the Torah to Jews who spoke only Ladino;56Rabbi Yaakov Culi was born in Jerusalem in 1689, moved to Constantinople, published the works of his teacher Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes (Mishneh LaMelech), and then began the Me’am Lo’ez in Ladino; he died in 1732 (NJOP). and Rabbi Chaim Palachi (1788–1868), chief rabbi of Izmir, wrote more than seventy works.57Rabbi Chaim Palachi (Izmir 1788–1868), Chacham Bashi of Izmir, author of more than seventy works, among them Lev Chaim, Nishmas Kol Chai and Tochachas Chaim (Wikipedia: Haim Palachi).

Persia is where Esther became queen, and Rav Tzadok says the palace of Achashverosh, for all its corruption, became “a dwelling for Esther’s holiness.”58Rav Tzadok explains that the outward modesty of the Persians, empty as it was, still gave Esther a place (Likkutei Maamarim, Festivals 16:10):
רַק לְפִי שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ הַגְּנוּת only because, out of the disgrace, זָכָה עַל כָּל פָּנִים he merited at least לִהְיוֹת בֵּיתוֹ מָעוֹן that his palace serve as a dwelling לִקְדוּשַּׁת אֶסְתֵּר, for Esther’s holiness, וְנַעֲשֵׂית לְמַלְכַּת פָּרַס. and she was made Queen of Persia. In modern times the Jews of Mashhad, forced to convert in 1839, lived as Muslims in public and kept Shabbos, kashrus and Torah in secret for almost a century, until they could live openly as Jews again.59In March 1839 a mob attacked the Jewish quarter of Mashhad and the survivors were forced to declare Islam. For almost a century they went to the mosque in public while keeping Shabbos, kashrus and prayer at home; women hid sifrei Torah and tefillin, and Rabbi Mordechai Akalar taught the children in secret. They could live openly as Jews from 1925 (Aish: The Secret Jews of Mashhad).

Pri Tzaddik’s “many daughters” include the other lands of exile, and the Gemara counts Torah scholars “from the rising of the sun to its setting” (Menachos 110a). From Yemen, at the southern end of the Arabian desert, came Rabbi Shalom Sharabi, the Rashash (1720–1777), who passed through India, Baghdad and Damascus on his way to Jerusalem and became the head of the Beis El kabbalists. Baghdad’s kabbalists, Rabbi Fatiyah and Rabbi Kaduri among them, prayed with his kavanos.60Rabbi Shalom Sharabi was born in 1720 in Sharab, Yemen, and died in Jerusalem in 1777. He became rosh yeshiva of the Beis El kabbalists, and his Siddur HaKavanos is still used by kabbalists in prayer and study (Wikipedia: Shalom Sharabi). From Morocco, at the far western edge of Yishmael’s lands, came the Baba Sali, Rabbi Yisrael Abuchatzeira (1889–1984), grandson of the Abir Yaakov.61Born in Rissani, Morocco, in 1889, the grandson of Rabbi Yaakov Abuchatzeira (the Abir Yaakov); he moved to Eretz Yisrael in 1951, returned for a time to lead the community in Morocco, settled in Netivot in 1964, and died there in 1984 (Wikipedia: Baba Sali). And the Chida, Rabbi Chaim Yosef David Azulai (1724–1806), born in Jerusalem to a family from Morocco, traveled as an emissary through Egypt, Tunisia and Morocco as well as Europe, and wrote some seventy works.62Born in Jerusalem in 1724, the great-great-grandson of the Moroccan kabbalist Rabbi Avraham Azulai. As an emissary of Chevron and Eretz Yisrael he traveled to Egypt, Tunisia, Morocco, Italy, Germany, France, Holland and England; he settled in Livorno, where he died in 1806. He wrote about seventy works, including Shem HaGedolim and Birkei Yosef (Wikipedia: Chaim Yosef David Azulai).

Strictly, only the first group comes from the lands of the Bnei Kedem: Bavel, Aram, Charan and Persia. Morocco is the far west, and the Chida was born in Eretz Yisrael. They belong to the second family of this shiur, Yishmael, whose kelipah Pri Tzaddik says “can be refined into holiness” (Part VIII), and to the “daughters” of the other lands who “did valiantly.”

Stories are told in our own generation of Jewish souls hidden inside Arab families who found their way back. They are stories, not documented history, and they are brought here as they are told, with their sources.

Rav Yitzchak Zilberstein tells, in Aleinu Leshabe’ach, of a young man raised as a Muslim in an Arab village in the Galilee. After a Yom Kippur in a shul in Kiryat Shemona he spoke to his mother, and she told him: “You are a Jew.” She came from a family rooted in Tzfas. He began to put on tefillin and came to a talmid chacham in Bnei Brak for Shabbos. Every time Lecha Dodi was sung, his eyes filled with tears, and he asked for it again and again. He showed his host an old photograph of his mother’s relatives praying at a grave in Tzfas. The next morning the host found the grave: it was the tomb of Rabbi Shlomo Alkabetz, who wrote Lecha Dodi.63The story appears in at least three versions, which agree on the core (a young man raised as a Muslim, a Jewish mother, tears at Lecha Dodi, and a link to Rabbi Shlomo Alkabetz) but differ in the details:
1. Rav Yitzchak Zilberstein, Aleinu Leshabe’ach, as told to him by a talmid chacham in Bnei Brak (the version above; retold in Shema Yisrael, Parshas Shelach). The young man is called Giaber Abu Chusein; his mother says his father was Druze; he worked in Kiryat Shemona.
2. Zev Roth, Monsey, Kiryat Sefer, and Beyond (Targum Press, 2002), “Coming Home from Ramallah” (Breslev Israel). Here he is “Machmud” from Ramallah, hosted in Jerusalem; his mother gives him her old Israeli identity card and the photograph from the grave. Roth writes: “The story is true; the names have been changed.”
3. Oded Mizrahi, “Yehudi BeDam” (abc770). Here “Mahmoud” from a Galilee village later takes the name Yehuda Alkabetz; he first sees Lecha Dodi in a siddur on Yom Kippur, learns in Bayit Vegan, and is married with the help of Rav Ovadia Yosef. His aunt’s family tradition is that they descend from “a great rabbi buried in Tzfas.”
None of the versions gives a date or details that can be checked, and the names differ. The descent from Rabbi Shlomo Alkabetz is the weakest part: a photograph of relatives praying at a tzaddik’s grave shows that they visited it, and many people pray there. What matters for halachah, and for this shiur, is the Jewish mother.
put on your garments of glory, my people;
draw near to my soul and redeem it.
Rav Tzadok explains how a Jewish soul can be born inside the house of an enemy and still return. He writes it about the descendants of Haman who taught Torah, but the rule is general.
taught Torah publicly in Bnei Brak…
that in my view it is clear
a man of the seed of Amalek
for converts are not accepted from Amalek…;
or some other case of force;
that the child is a kosher Jew…
there is an absorbing, even from Amalek,
to blot out that holy seed,
the son of a Jewish woman,

Two more stories of the same kind have been reported in our time. Mark Halawa was born in Kuwait to a Palestinian Muslim family. He grew up knowing that his mother’s mother had been a Jew in Jerusalem, without knowing what it meant, until a Jewish professor in Canada told him that it made him Jewish. He moved to Jerusalem, learned in yeshiva, married, and lives there as an observant Jew.64Deborah Danan, “An Arab Comes Home to His Judaism,” Jewish Journal, March 28, 2018 (Jewish Journal). He learned at the University of Western Ontario that his maternal grandmother’s Jewishness made him Jewish, and later made Arabic-language videos explaining Israel to the Arab world. And a young man in Jordan, called “Ahmed” in the report, whose mother and grandmother were Jews from Iraq, from Bavel, learned by chance from a video of the religious singer Ziv Yechezkel that Jewishness passes through the mother. He contacted Yad L’Achim, which sends him books on Judaism in Arabic, and he keeps his Judaism secret for fear of those around him. The organization said it had received similar requests from some 150 people across the Muslim world in a year and a half.65World Israel News, July 31, 2019, citing Ma’ariv (World Israel News). The account comes from Yad L’Achim and from Ahmed’s interview; it was not independently checked. In the same year Israel Hayom reported a man from a family of hidden Jews in an Arab country with no ties to Israel who lit Chanukah candles in secret (Israel Hayom, December 27, 2019).
For contrast: in 1928 Yitzchak Ben-Zvi, later Israel’s second president, recorded that the Makhamra clan of Yatta, near Chevron, said “We the Makhamra are from the seed of Jews” and avoided camel meat (She’ar Yeshuv); a 1938 report in the Palestine Post described families in Yatta lighting Chanukah candles obtained from the Jews of Chevron. Their tradition traces Jewish descent through the fathers, many generations back, and its origin is disputed; they have remained Muslims (Wikipedia: Makhamra family).

In every one of these stories the way back runs through a Jewish mother, exactly as Rav Tzadok explains: the son of a Jewish woman is “a kosher Israelite,” a holy seed that cannot be blotted out. And in each one something small of Torah stayed alive inside Yishmael’s house, a song of Shabbos, a grandmother’s name, a Chanukah light, until the soul recognized it. Memories of Jewish customs kept by families whose Jewish ancestry ran only through the fathers, centuries back, have not brought them back in the same way.
